item.title: Future Management — Innovation and Work
item.description:
Does AI Assistance Enhance or Erode Expertise? Evidence from a Three-Month Field Experiment in Patent Drafting
David Autor et al.
NBER Working Paper, September 2026 

Abstract:

Whether AI assistance builds or erodes professional expertise is unsettled. In a pre-registered three-month randomized controlled trial, we gave 133 practicing patent lawyers at eleven U.S. intellectual property law firms access to a custom AI drafting assistant and measured both their performance while using AI and their professional judgment afterward without it. All work was scored by blinded expert patent attorneys. Paralleling findings from other white-collar domains, AI access raised the quality of work delivered on benchmark patent drafting tasks at 10 days (0.34 SD, p = 0.03) and 90 days (0.38 SD, p = 0.01), with larger gains among junior lawyers. After three months, all subjects redlined an existing patent application without AI, a core task of patent practice requiring expert judgment. Treated lawyers outperformed controls by 0.32 SD (p = 0.04), but this advantage was concentrated entirely among senior lawyers (0.45 SD, p = 0.02). Junior lawyers showed no average gain; their scores instead bifurcated, with sharply fewer mediocre scores offset by more poor and more good ones. The largest gains from AI thus accrued to the lawyers who retained the least. Foundational expertise may be a prerequisite for extracting durable skill from AI-assisted practice.

The First Draft Problem: Productivity, Quality, and Physiological Strain in LLM-Assisted Writing
Xufei Liu, Hummy Song & Christian Terwiesch
University of Pennsylvania Working Paper, September 2026 

Abstract:

The use of large language models (LLMs) has grown rapidly over the past few years, especially in health care, where documentation burden remains a persistent problem for practicing clinicians. However, despite the deployment of many ambient scribes for documentation, it is still unclear how LLMs impact those who work with them. Across two preregistered studies, we examine how this shift -- from writing documentation to editing an LLM-generated draft -- impacts workers. We study this "first draft problem": eliminating the blank page does not remove the work of documentation but relocates it into revising and editing. In Study 1, an online experiment with 16 clinicians producing documentation following a teletherapy patient encounter, we establish the puzzle: counter to our hypotheses, editing an LLM-generated draft of the documentation as opposed to writing it from scratch does not result in time savings or quality improvements on average. Instead, while some clinicians experience no time savings but large improvements in quality after making substantial revisions, others experience meaningful time savings and no change in quality after making limited revisions. In other words, we observe significant heterogeneity in how clinicians engage with the same draft, which leads to variation in productivity and quality. In Study 2, a lab experiment with 100 university students summarizing video interviews, we unpack the mechanisms underlying this heterogeneity using granular keystroke logs, validated self-reports of workload, and micro-level physiological and eye-tracking measurements. In this setting, we find the expected productivity improvements: editing reduces task completion time by roughly 70%, raises quality, and lowers self-reported workload. Yet the physiological evidence tells a more nuanced story. Physiological markers indicate that fatigue accumulates faster when editing an LLM-generated draft than when writing from scratch. Thus, we find that (a) time savings can be real, but are setting dependent; (b) quality improvements are possible, but the relationship between how heavily a draft is revised and the quality of the result differs sharply across our two settings; and (c) while editing an LLM draft lowers reported cognitive load, the body still tires faster over time.

Is the job-hopping penalty merited? Predicting selection decisions, turnover, and performance of job hoppers
Jake Harrison et al.
Journal of Applied Psychology, forthcoming

Abstract:

Despite the prevalence of job hopping in the modern world of work, it remains unclear whether penalizing applicants with a history of job hopping is merited. We conducted four studies to investigate the extent of the job-hopping penalty in the selection process and whether that penalty is merited when predicting turnover and performance. In Study 1, we reviewed definitions and gathered insights from human resource practitioners (N = 61) to offer a refined definition of job hopping. In Study 2, we implemented an experimental hiring scenario and found that hiring managers (N = 85) consistently rated job-hopping applicants lower than non-job-hopping applicants and that this occurred, in part, through lower expected commitment and performance. Although career progression did not weaken the impact of job hopping on application evaluations through expected commitment and performance, it did weaken the direct impact of job hopping on application evaluations. In Study 3, we analyzed data from job applicants for a sales position (N = 30,640) and found that job hopping related to fewer job offers, higher turnover, and lower job performance and predicted these outcomes beyond other selection procedures (e.g., a situational judgment test). Further, prehire experience moderated (weakened) the negative relationship between job hopping and job offers. In Study 4, we replicated these findings in a sample of job applicants for a retail manager position (N = 37,105). Together, these studies show that job hoppers are penalized, the penalty is warranted, and career progression and prehire experience can weaken the impact of the penalty.

Remote work and effort provision in teams
Glenn Dutcher & Krista Saral
Economic Journal, forthcoming

Abstract:

Remote work policies remain controversial partly because of productivity concerns, which are potentially exacerbated in team settings. Using experiments, we isolate how location-based beliefs of teammate effort affect the own-effort choices of participants assigned to work with remote and office-based teammates. Participants perform a real effort task and can contribute this effort to an individual account, paying a piece rate wage, or to a team account using a minimum-effort payment scheme. We find that remote workers do not complete fewer tasks than their office-based counterparts. Yet, teams suffer from lower effort due to workers responding to beliefs that remote teammates contribute less effort to the team. In a follow-up treatment, we demonstrate that these location-based beliefs remain salient even under a revenue-sharing team payment scheme where beliefs of free-riding may have dominated. Finally, we provide unique evidence that the COVID-19 pandemic may have shifted beliefs to be more pessimistic about the effort of remote workers but did not alter the actual effort.

When Does Randomized Oversight Align AI Agents That Can Conceal?
Joshua Gans & Richard Holden
NBER Working Paper, October 2026 

Abstract:

Oversight changes the evidence it relies on. We ask when randomized audits and scoring align AI agents that can conceal misconduct and alter records. Stronger auditing makes undeterred violations better hidden. Because the provider writes the agent's objective, sanctions need not stop at forfeiture, and rare audits deter every type of agent if evidence survives concealment and audit draws cannot be learned in advance. When evidence can be erased, deterrence must come from lower gains from violation, such as credit for stopping, or from costlier or fewer ways to conceal. These conditions identify what failed when agents in OpenAI's cybersecurity evaluations compromised parts of Hugging Face's infrastructure in July 2026.

Asking open-ended questions promotes personal goal attainment in integrative negotiations
Matteo Di Stasi, Alison Wood Brooks & Jordi Quoidbach
Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, October 2026, Pages 2435-2453

Abstract:

Prior research suggests that asking more questions improves outcomes in cooperative conversations, and a vast wisdom literature espouses the power of asking questions during conflictual conversations, too: Negotiation experts suggest that questions invite counterparts to disclose information and, in doing so, put askers at an informational advantage. But is this advice necessary -- and is it effective? We analyzed 61,057 speech turns from transcripts of 309 dyadic integrative negotiations and used natural language processing to estimate how often people ask questions, what types of questions they ask, and how well question-asking predicts personal goal attainment (Study 1; n = 618 MBA students). Open-ended questions were rare, occurring about once every 4 min (8% of turns). Yet, asking more open-ended questions was robustly associated with personal gains. Closed-ended questions and nonquestion statements were not reliably related to personal gains. We then tested causality in live chat negotiations: Participants who were instructed to ask open-ended questions achieved higher personal gains than those instructed to ask closed-ended questions or to only make statements (Study 2; n = 1,452 online participants), and those instructed to prepare open-ended questions before their interactions outperformed those instructed to prepare statements (Study 3; n = 372 online participants). In all studies, the benefits of open-ended questions were tied to increased information elicitation and greater value creation. Collectively, these findings offer empirical support for the widely accepted-but rarely tested-claim that negotiators (and conversationalists broadly) focus excessively on influencing (by making statements) at the expense of learning (by asking questions).

When Are Two Heads Better than One? The Organizational Design of Innovation
Felix Feng et al.
University of Georgia Working Paper, October 2026 

Abstract:

We study the optimal allocation of tasks over the life cycle of an innovative project. Innovation requires two complementary activities, research and development, both subject to moral hazard. Agents also privately observe the quality of discoveries, so the principal must elicit truthful reports to avoid costly mistakes. Assigning both tasks to a single "solo operator" avoids free-riding but creates a double-deviation problem: the agent can shirk on research and conceal the resulting low-quality discovery. As time passes without a discovery, this deviation becomes increasingly attractive. Separating the tasks across two agents eliminates the double deviation but introduces free-riding. We characterize how this tradeoff shapes organization over time. When low-quality discoveries are readily exposed, the project is run by sequential solo operators; when they are difficult to expose, a two-agent team is optimal from the outset. At intermediate levels of detectability, the project begins with a solo operator and switches endogenously to a team.

Knowledge protection and modularity of innovation activities in firms: Evidence from US trade secrecy law
Eunkwang Seo & Christopher Dinkel
Strategic Management Journal, forthcoming 

Abstract:

Strategy scholars have theoretically explored the relationship between legal knowledge protection and modularity of innovation activities in firms, but this relationship has yet to be empirically tested in the literature. Leveraging state-level changes in US trade secrecy law and using a network modularity measure, this paper examines how trade secret protection affects the modularity of firms' innovation activities. Analyzing intrafirm inventor collaboration patterns in US patent data from 783 high-tech firms between 1976 and 2017, we find that increased trade secret protection is negatively associated with the modularity of innovation activities within firms. This effect is more pronounced for firms with superior technologies and those geographically collocated with competitors -- factors that enhance firms' knowledge appropriability concerns -- and less pronounced for firms in industries where alternative appropriability mechanisms are highly effective. Moreover, our findings suggest that the increased betweenness centrality of new hires (skilled and junior) serves as an important underlying mechanism for the treatment effect. These results contribute to the literature by illuminating how firms strategize their internal innovation activities for knowledge protection and by underscoring its underlying mechanism.

item.title: Agents in Government — Legislative Institutions
item.description:
Checks, Balances, and Presidential Ambitions
Christian Fong, Kenneth Lowande & Ayse Eldes
Quarterly Journal of Political Science, September 2026, Pages 249-288

Abstract:
This study investigates the relationship between running for president and members’ contributions to the core legislative functions that impact Congress’s standing relative to the presidency. This study finds some evidence that ambitious legislators attend roll call votes and oversight hearings at lower rates, but at the same time, they are more legislatively productive, conduct just as much informal oversight and are equally informational in their public oversight. When Congress votes on an issue that affects the balance of power between Congress and the president, they are more likely to side with Congress than legislators without presidential ambitions are. These behavioral differences persist even after their presidential runs, which suggests they are not driven by a strategic effort to audition for the presidency.

The Convergence of Zero-Sum Thinking and Illiberalism in the United States
Jacob Morrier, Beatrice Magistro & Michael Alvarez
Social Science Quarterly, September 2026

Methods: In a nationally representative survey experiment (n = 2397), we asked respondents whether existential threats justify restricting fundamental rights under one of three randomized issue frames: climate change (a liberal issue), illegal immigration (a conservative issue), or no specific threat.

Results: We find that zero-sum thinking strongly predicts support for illiberal attitudes across all treatment conditions: an interquartile-range increase in zero-sum thinking is associated with an 11–13 percentage point increase in illiberal attitudes, regardless of partisan affiliation. Framing effects are confined to low zero-sum thinkers, who respond predictably to partisan cues: Democrats favor restrictions for climate change, while Republicans do so when they address illegal immigration. High zero-sum thinkers, by contrast, hit a “threat ceiling,” exhibiting uniformly high support for coercive measures with little sensitivity to partisan framing.

Debate and Legislative Productivity in US State Legislatures
Nicholas Howard & Tessa Provins
Legislative Studies Quarterly, November 2026

Abstract:
Scholarship holds that procedural rules shape legislative proceedings, but most existing evidence comes from the US Congress' limited procedural variation. This article develops a theoretical framework for how different forms of debate restriction -- both limits on member participation and procedural hurdles to closing debate -- affect legislative productivity, and how these effects depend on chambers' institutional capacity. Using an original dataset of debate rules and bill progression spanning 2011–2018 from all 99 US state legislative chambers, we show that restrictions on member speaking opportunities and ending debate are associated with higher legislative productivity, with the relationship operating through distinct mechanisms. Procedural hurdles to ending debate are associated with higher productivity in low-professionalism legislatures, while these associations diminish or reverse in more professionalized chambers. These findings demonstrate the conditional nature of debate rules and institutional capacity, offering new insight into procedural designs and the tradeoff between deliberation and efficiency in lawmaking.

“Congruence” and “Responsiveness” in the study of representation
John Matsusaka
Public Choice, September 2026, Pages 589-602

Abstract:
This paper compares two common methods used to measure representation in empirical research: “congruence,” whether a roll-call vote is aligned with constituent opinion; and “responsiveness,” the correlation between roll-call votes and constituent opinion. While sometimes viewed as different ways of capturing the same underlying concept of “representation,” theoretically the measures are not connected. This paper assesses to what extent responsiveness and congruence capture the same thing empirically. Using 4,192 roll-call votes on 33 state laws that were subsequently challenged in referendums, I calculate both congruence and responsiveness for the same set of votes. The main finding is that responsiveness is an unreliable predictor of congruence, and therefore cannot be taken as a proxy for congruence.

Legislative Financial Asset Disclosure, Firm Motivations, and Macroeconomic Outcomes in the US States
Justin Kirkland & Patrick Shea
Regulation & Governance, forthcoming

Abstract:
Financial asset disclosure laws are widely implemented to combat conflicts of interest among policymakers, yet their economic impact remains poorly understood. This study provides the first comprehensive analysis of how these transparency measures affect macroeconomic outcomes across the 50 US states. We theorize that these disclosure and recusal laws could have divergent impacts on macroeconomic performance: they might enhance economic outcomes by curtailing the exploitation of political connections by business firms, or conversely, they could impede economic growth by altering firm behavior and deterring business leaders from seeking public office, thereby potentially reducing the pool of economically savvy policymakers. Using new data on state-level disclosure policies, we find that asset disclosure laws are associated with a worsening macroeconomic environment in states. To uncover the mechanisms driving these counterintuitive results, we conduct two pre-registered survey experiments with 2000 small business owners. Our experimental evidence suggests that stringent disclosure requirements deter business investment and expansion. This research has implications for legislative challenges for legislative design, transparency, and economic policy.

Location, Location, Location: Senate Trading and Seat Proximity
Dane Christensen et al.
Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, forthcoming

Abstract:
Using the distance between two Senators’ desks to capture the proclivity to share information, we find that when two Senators sit closer together in the Senate Chamber, they are more likely to trade stocks in the same industry and earn larger returns, especially when they belong to the same political party. This association varies with Senators’ information sources and power, and the scrutiny they face. We perform multiple identification tests to support our inference that Senators share private trading information gleaned from their positions in Congress. Moreover, we provide the first evidence on the career benefits associated with sharing information.

Institutional insulation as response to racial diversity: Evidence from the Great Migration
Jacob Grumbach, Robert Mickey & Daniel Ziblatt
Journal of Historical Political Economy, September 2026, Pages 171-196

Abstract:
Democratic institutions in the US federal system are decentralized, and lower-level governments have the potential to counteract national democratization. The authors argue that, in response to growing Black electoral power resulting from the Great Migration, northern cities moved to insulate governmental institutions from their diversifying electorates. Using a shift-share instrument, the authors find that greater migration of Black Americans from the South between 1940 and 1970 led cities to switch from mayor-council to city manager systems, shifting the administration of local government, including budgeting and bureaucratic hiring, out of the direct control of elected officials. The authors illustrate how the Great Migration shaped the decision of city elites to switch to city manager government through a case study of Santa Monica, CA. The findings speak to the importance of considering multilevel governance in assessing democratic trends.

Old Times There Are Not Forgotten: The Legacy of Southern Populism for Public Goods Provision
Daniel Blinderman
Studies in American Political Development, October 2026, Pages 253-279

Abstract:
Why did the states of the Jim Crow South vary in both their overall level and geographic distribution of public goods? Christian Fong, Kenneth Lowande & Ayse Eldes
Quarterly Journal of Political Science, September 2026, Pages 249-288

Abstract:
This study investigates the relationship between running for president and members’ contributions to the core legislative functions that impact Congress’s standing relative to the presidency. This study finds some evidence that ambitious legislators attend roll call votes and oversight hearings at lower rates, but at the same time, they are more legislatively productive, conduct just as much informal oversight and are equally informational in their public oversight. When Congress votes on an issue that affects the balance of power between Congress and the president, they are more likely to side with Congress than legislators without presidential ambitions are. These behavioral differences persist even after their presidential runs, which suggests they are not driven by a strategic effort to audition for the presidency.

The Convergence of Zero-Sum Thinking and Illiberalism in the United States
Jacob Morrier, Beatrice Magistro & Michael Alvarez
Social Science Quarterly, September 2026

Methods: In a nationally representative survey experiment (n = 2397), we asked respondents whether existential threats justify restricting fundamental rights under one of three randomized issue frames: climate change (a liberal issue), illegal immigration (a conservative issue), or no specific threat.

Abstract:

Shruti Jha et al.

Abstract:

This result is consonant with parental and school investments acting as substitutes in skill production. Because this latent parental capacity pays off precisely when school inputs fail, standard measurement tools for early childhood programs can miss crucial state-contingent value.

Public perceptions of polygenic testing and embryo selection for non-medical traits
Edmond Awad et al.
Nature Human Behaviour, forthcoming

Abstract:
Some advances in reproductive technologies raise substantial ethical and psychological challenges, for example, the use of preimplantation genetic testing to select embryos based on non-medical traits. While studies have explored public willingness to use preimplantation genetic testing for medical or non-medical attributes, stated willingness may not reflect implantation decisions when such information is available. This large cross-national study examined public views on polygenic embryo testing. In a US sample (N = 1,467), participants were more willing to test for medical conditions (for example, heart disease) than non-medical traits (for example, antisocial behaviour or low intelligence), although over half supported testing for non-medical traits. In a forced-choice implantation task, participants used medical and non-medical information to a similar extent when making decisions. Similar patterns were observed in Chinese participants (N = 623). These findings suggest variability in choices across specific traits and conditions, rather than a uniform distinction between medical conditions and non-medical traits.

Riley Steiner, Brooke Whitfield & Laura Lindberg
Journal of Sex Research, forthcoming

Abstract:
In the context of increasing restrictions on sexual and reproductive health care, inadequate sex education, and increasing antihormonal contraceptive sentiment, we examined post-coital pregnancy prevention behavior among a nationally representative sample of U.S. adolescents and young adults (AYA). We developed a novel measure of post-coital contraceptive strategies (i.e., actions taken after sexual intercourse with the intent of reducing the likelihood of pregnancy) and fielded this measure for the first time as part of a 2025 online, population-based survey of English-speaking 15–29-year-olds assigned female at birth (n = 1,259). Of the 633 AYA who reported having ever had penile-vaginal sex and were not currently pregnant, 25.0% used at least one post-coital strategy to prevent pregnancy the last time they had sex. While methods with established effectiveness (i.e., emergency contraception and copper intrauterine device) were used by 8.9% respondents, 16.1% reported using a non-medically evidenced post-coital strategy, the most common being praying (9.4%). Post-coital strategy use varied by age, race and ethnicity, and number of contraceptive methods used. In multivariable analyses, contraceptive knowledge was negatively associated with post-coital strategy use. Regardless of effectiveness, post-coital strategies are common enough to warrant inclusion in behavioral surveillance and attention in health education and clinical practice.

James Rilling et al.
Psychoneuroendocrinology, forthcoming

Abstract:
Previous cross-sectional studies have documented hormonal differences between human fathers and nonfathers. However, the timing and persistence of these changes remain unclear. We previously reported that first-time expecting fathers exhibited lower plasma testosterone (T) and arginine vasopressin (AVP), as well as dynamic changes in oxytocin (OT) across portions of the prenatal and early postpartum period compared with partnered nonfather controls. By four months postpartum, however, these group differences were no longer significant. Here, we extend these findings longitudinally into late infancy and early childhood. After controlling for relevant confounds, plasma T, OT, AVP and cortisol levels did not differ significantly between fathers and nonfathers at either one or two years postpartum. Nevertheless, individual differences in paternal hormone levels continued to predict paternal behavior and relationship functioning. At one year postpartum, lower T was associated with greater paternal positive engagement and less frustration with the child, whereas higher cortisol was associated with lower paternal positive engagement. At two years postpartum, higher OT was associated with stronger father-infant attachment. Both fathers and their partners reported declining relationship quality across this period, and mediation analyses suggested that higher T levels mediated the association between reduced time spent with partners and poorer relationship quality. These findings suggest that hormonal changes accompanying the transition to fatherhood may be transient at the group level, while individual variation in paternal hormones continue to relate meaningfully to caregiving, attachment, and relationship functioning into early childhood.

Nicole Oppenheimer, Lori Reider & Vanessa LoBue
Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, December 2026

Abstract:

One potential pathway by which pets might encourage the development of empathy is through the use of emotional and mental state (EMST) language during conversations about pets. These findings provide some of the first experimental evidence that a single brief exposure to a representation of a real dog encourages greater use of EMST language in parent–child interactions -- language that is associated with children’s positive social-emotional development.

item.title: Intelligent Marketing — Algorithms and Information
item.description:
Artists Can Design Memory, and AI Can Predict It
Trent Davis, Yifei Chen & Wilma Bainbridge
Psychological Science, forthcoming

Abstract:
Can artists deliberately design artworks to be remembered -- or forgotten? Across three experiments, we tested whether visual-memory outcomes can be shaped through artistic design and how they are predicted by artists, laypeople, and artificial intelligence. We launched a nationwide art contest in which artists submitted works intended to be memorable or forgettable. Using recognition tasks with adults based in the United States (119 from Amazon Mechanical Turk, 892 from Prolific, and 62 visitors from a Chicago gallery), we found that artists achieved their intended memory outcomes. However, their success was asymmetric: Memorability was more readily increased than reduced. A neural network, ResMem, consistently outperformed human observers and artists in predicting which artworks would be remembered. Data-driven analyses identified psychologically interpretable features that explained nearly half the variance in memory and aligned with ResMem's predictions, but not with human judgments. Together, findings suggest that visual memorability can be engineered by humans, though asymmetrically, and is better captured by computational models.

Myopic Expansions on Digital Platforms
Ahmadreza Mostajabi, Aldona Kapacinskaite & Keyvan Vakili
Administrative Science Quarterly, forthcoming

Abstract:
Digitization has enabled modern firms to expand at unprecedented rates, but there are downsides to rapid expansion. Prior research has highlighted how digital platforms facilitate mass-market expansions by resolving frictions associated with market entry. Accordingly, various studies have emphasized the positive impact of market-friction reduction on aggregate market size and efficiency. In this article, we argue that the extreme resolution of frictions may also have a downside: It can nudge platform participants to overlook the heterogeneous nature of different markets and, consequently, to engage in large-scale, potentially myopic market expansions. These expansions, in turn, may engender lower customer satisfaction and firm performance. We test our arguments in the context of Apple's App Store. We find that apps that undergo rapid, large-scale market expansions, relative to apps that do not expand or that expand more gradually, see a short-run increase in client base but longer-run declines in ratings, downloads, financial performance, and innovation. By addressing the underexplored negative side of resolving market frictions on platforms, the study advances knowledge of digital strategy and scaling.

The Challenges of Deploying an Algorithmic Pricing Tool: Evidence from Airbnb
Mohsen Foroughifar & Nitin Mehta
Marketing Science, forthcoming

Abstract:
We examine the challenges of deploying an artificial intelligence pricing tool, Smart Pricing (SP), developed by Airbnb to assist hosts in pricing their properties. SP was made available free of charge and was intended to benefit hosts that rarely adjusted their prices in response to temporal demand fluctuations. However, SP's adoption rate was low, particularly among hosts who rarely changed their prices prior to SP's introduction. We estimate a structural model to (i) identify the extent to which adoption costs, hosts' pessimistic prior beliefs about SP's performance, and suboptimality of SP contributed to its low adoption rate and (ii) suggest ways to improve SP's adoption rate that would in turn increase Airbnb's and hosts' profitability. We find that (a) the main reason for SP's low adoption rate is hosts' pessimistic prior beliefs about SP's performance, which are stronger among hosts who rarely changed their prices; (b) the benefits of SP for hosts and Airbnb can be increased if Airbnb were to educate the hosts about SP's actual performance; and (c) because Airbnb does not have information on hosts' marginal costs, retraining SP using the structural estimates of marginal costs can substantially increase Airbnb's and hosts' profitability.

Isha Agarwal, Wentong Chen & Eswar Prasad
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
When does bad news stick? This paper shows that the persistence of media sentiment depends not only on whether news is good or bad, but also on what the news is about. Using the complete Wall Street Journal archive from 1990 to 2025, we construct monthly positive and negative sentiment indices for twelve economic topics and estimate topic-specific sentiment dynamics. Bad-news innovations generate larger cumulative responses than positive-sentiment innovations in every topic, indicating that negativity asymmetry is a broad feature of media sentiment. But the size of this asymmetry varies sharply across topics. The bad-minus-positive persistence gap is largest in security and human rights, firms and corporate strategy, health and public safety, and real estate and financial stability. Bad-news persistence is also sizable in data-rich topics such as financial markets, real estate, and corporate news, suggesting that frequent information arrival does not necessarily lead narratives to revert quickly. These findings show that aggregate sentiment indices mask substantial topic-level heterogeneity in the asymmetric dynamics of narratives, with potential implications for how persistent negative sentiment shapes expectations, asset prices, and real economic outcomes.

Greenwashing in Earnings Conference Calls
Luzi Hail, Shawn Kim & Rachel Xi Zhang
University of Pennsylvania Working Paper, July 2026

Abstract:
We examine the presence, use, and consequences of corporate greenwashing in earnings conference calls for a large sample of U.S. firms from 2008 to 2022. We develop a measure of greenwashing as the absolute difference between the actual and a model-based expected level of climate change discussions by management. To validate our proxy, we show that the abnormal (greenwashing) component does not convey material information about concurrent and future environmental performance, while the predicted component does. Greenwashing is widespread, has increased over time, and responds to reporting incentives such as high-profile environmental scandals and disasters. When it comes to potential benefits, we find that capital markets do not price greenwashing, consistent with investors not being fooled by this overly optimistic communication. However, we do find near-term reputational benefits of greenwashing in the form of a more positive sentiment towards the firm as expressed in environmental ratings, news articles, blog entries, and social media posts. Our results suggest that corporate greenwashing may be less aimed at capital markets but rather at other important stakeholders beyond investors.

item.description:
Real-World Brinkmanship In Hospital-Insurer Negotiations
Jason Buxbaum, Neil Mehta & Andrew Ryan
Health Affairs, October 2026, Pages 1078-1087

Abstract:

Threats of network departicipation (brinkmanship) in these negotiations may help parties secure more favorable terms. We studied 14,918 relationships between 3,772 unique hospitals and 92 unique in-market insurers to better understand the relationships among organizational characteristics (including market conditions), public brinkmanship, and departicipation. We documented 1,249 episodes of public brinkmanship, corresponding to about 8 percent of hospital-insurer relationships, for contracts ending between August 2021 and July 2025. About 28 percent of these public threats culminated in withdrawal. Profitable hospitals, for-profit hospitals, and hospitals commanding relatively high prices were most likely to engage in public brinkmanship; national insurers were more likely to engage in brinkmanship than single-state or regional insurers. We observed brinkmanship in about 16 percent of relationships where the hospital system and insurer each controlled roughly 25-45 percent and 30-45 percent of local beds and commercial lives, respectively. Our findings emphasize the importance of local contexts in shaping hospital-insurer relationships. Conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence in ambulatory primary care: A prospective feasibility study
Peter Brodeur et al.
The Lancet, forthcoming

Methods: In this prospective, single-centre, single-arm feasibility study, English-speaking patients aged at least 18 years interacted with the Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer (AMIE) up to 5 days before a single-complaint urgent primary care appointment. Physician safety supervisors monitored all interactions and were trained to intervene on the basis of predefined safety criteria. AMIE transcripts and summaries were shared with PCPs before the visit. Primary outcomes were the number of supervised conversation safety stops, AMIE's conversation quality assessed by clinical evaluators, and patient and PCP experiences per surveys. Zero conversation safety stops were required on the basis of prespecified criteria. Safety supervisors noted one hallucination and added clinical information in five interactions. AMIE's conversations were rated favourably in 87-100% of cases (17 criteria) by clinical evaluators, and 48-96% (16 criteria) by patients. Patient attitudes towards AI improved after interacting with AMIE and remained elevated after the patient's visit with their physician. PCPs completed post-surveys in 60 of 98 cases, including 44 cases in which they reviewed the AMIE transcript before the visit. Public Service Decline and Support for the Populist Right: Evidence from England's National Health Service
Zachary Dickson et al.
American Political Science Review, forthcoming

Abstract:
The rise of populist right parties is well studied, but relatively little attention has been given to how public service performance influences voter support. Given that public services are often the primary means through which citizens interact with the state, we argue that declining public services can create grievances that increase the appeal of populist right parties. Focusing on England's National Health Service, we combine administrative data on local health facility closures with panel data on public preferences and voting intentions. Ian McCarthy & Katie Leinenbach
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
The Critical Access Hospital (CAH) program, established under the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, provides cost-based Medicare reimbursement to small rural hospitals in exchange for limits on inpatient capacity and service scope. We find that CAH designation raises operating margins by three to four percentage points, with no change in liquidity or capital investment, as cost-based reimbursement sustains revenue while expenses fall with scale. Designation also reduces inpatient scale, with significant declines in total beds, obstetric capacity, and nursing staff. Emergency department visits also decline meaningfully, while outpatient volume is largely unchanged. At the same time, CAH designation reduces hospital closures, with no meaningful effect on mergers. These results point to a "survival versus scale" tradeoff across hospitals within a state, wherein designation-based subsidies avert closure for a small number of hospitals while inducing widespread inpatient downsizing among the many more hospitals that convert. Daniel Arnold et al.
NBER Working Paper, August 2026

Abstract:
The diffusion of technological innovation depends on incentives, regulations, and firms' strategic behaviors. We study these intersections within cardiac procedure markets following Medicare's expansion of non-hospital facility options for treatment, enabled by clinical advancements. State-level regulations restrain federal pro-competition policy. Where market entry occurs, business stealing is concentrated among the lowest cost treatment settings, rather than high-cost hospitals -- increasing Medicare spending by approximately $2.5 million. Medicare policy also generates externalities for untargeted procedures and other payers, except when hospitals and physicians are vertically integrated. Federal rulemaking interacts with and is mitigated by complex market dynamics -- including in potentially unanticipated ways.

Understanding (Gender) Bias in Psychiatric Diagnosis: The Case of ADHD
Anke Bueter
Philosophy of Science, October 2026, Pages 792-812

Abstract:
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is diagnosed more often in males than females. Recently, this gap has narrowed, a development often framed as overcoming gender bias. This framing rests on two problematic assumptions: (1) more equal diagnostic rates approximate truth and (2) there is such a truth in the first place. Assumption (1) is questionable because male populations are set as standard but potentially reflect overdiagnosis. Assumption (2) presumes ADHD to be a stable, discrete disease entity, which is epistemically and ontologically problematic. I argue that understanding (gender) bias here should focus on deviations from best practices and deliberative norms rather than a relation to truth.

Avoiding Regulation: Evidence from Nursing Homes
Alden Cheng & Riley League
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
We study strategic responses by firms to threshold-based regulations. We document extensive bunching in response to additional staffing requirements for California nursing homes with at least 100 beds. We estimate that higher staffing above the threshold is nearly entirely due to selection, with low-staffing facilities manipulating their size to avoid the regulation. Michael Rovito & Derek Griffith
American Journal of Preventive Medicine, October 2026

Abstract:
In November 2025, Denver Broncos linebacker Alex Singleton's accidental testicular cancer diagnosis through routine drug testing highlighted a critical gap in detection guidance for young men. Despite being the most common malignancy among males aged 15 to 44, the United States Preventive Services Task Force maintains a D recommendation against testicular self-examination (TSE), effectively discouraging awareness and discussion. This recommendation, unchanged for over two decades and based on outdated evidence, conflicts with guidance from urological societies like the European Association of Urology and American Urological Association, which support counseling and education for high-risk populations. The inconsistency creates confusion for clinicians and patients alike. Current evidence shows that individual detection through palpation remains the most common route to diagnosis, yet young men face structural barriers to healthcare access, limited touchpoints with providers, and profound knowledge gaps about testicular cancer. The USPSTF's narrow focus on mortality data ignores broader impacts including the dramatic survival rate differences between early-stage (99%) and distant disease (69-74%), as well as disruptions to education, employment, and fertility when diagnosis is delayed. Reclassifying the recommendation from D (recommend against) to I (insufficient evidence) would more accurately reflect the evidence, remove barriers to clinical discussion, and enable health systems to engage young men through school programs, college health centers, and primary care encounters. Health Affairs, October 2026, Pages 1088-1095

Of the 639 health systems in the United States in 2023, 179 (28.0 percent) offered an insurance plan, most often Medicare Advantage plans. Across health care services, forty-four of forty-six had negotiated prices that were significantly lower for provider-sponsored health plans compared with those for nonintegrated insurance plans. These findings offer evidence that provider-sponsored health plans negotiate health care prices with their health systems differently than nonintegrated insurers do, but greater transparency in pricing and ownership is essential to fully assess the risks and benefits that provider-sponsored health plans may have for health care prices.

Expansions in scope of practice provider regulations for certified nurse midwives & maternal-infant health outcomes: Evidence from PRAMS
Agnitra Roy Choudhury, Alicia Plemmons & Sriparna Ghosh
Journal of Regulatory Economics, October 2026

Abstract:
Growing shortages in women's health care providers can delay prenatal care, increasing risks for both mothers and infants. To address this, many states have expanded regulations on non-physician practice authority, allowing certified nurse midwives to deliver a wider range of services, independent of direct physician supervision. Supporters argue that these expansions can help fill provider gaps and improve access to early prenatal care. Critics question whether the quality of care might decline without physician oversight. Despite growing policy interest, there is limited evidence on how independent practice affects maternal and infant health. This study examines the impact of practice reforms for Certified Nurse Midwives on health outcomes with data from the Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System. Using a difference-in-differences approach, we find that regulatory expansions in the autonomy of Certified Nurse Midwives lead to earlier prenatal care without negatively affecting birth outcomes. Our findings suggest that regulatory flexibility can improve access to care without compromising quality.

item.title: How Moral — Values and Judgment
item.description:
Change perception at zero tolerance: How protected values bias sensitivity to social improvement
Tobias Vogel & André Mata
Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, forthcoming

Abstract:
Across six experiments, we examined how sensitivity to change varies with protected values (PVs). In Experiment 1, vegetarians were less appreciative than meat-eaters of large (but only partial) reductions in other people’s meat consumption, but they were more appreciative than meat-eaters of smaller but absolute reductions (i.e., reduction to zero meat consumption). In Experiment 2, a similar pattern emerged in political groups: Republicans, who value immigration control more than Democrats, were relatively less sensitive to large but partial reductions in illegal immigration than to its elimination; the reverse pattern was observed for gun possession. In Experiment 3, we manipulated participants’ values regarding child labor. Individuals who generated arguments in defense of child labor held less protected values and were comparatively more sensitive to change in child labor numbers. Further studies showed that protected values make people focus on the outcome (i.e., the present state) more than on the trajectory of change (i.e., the difference from the past; Experiment 4) and that they inspire stricter thresholds for what is considered acceptable (Experiment 5). Experiment 6 shows that protected values cause a heightened sensitivity to absolute changes to zero, rather than insensitivity to changes overall. These findings indicate that protected values amplify sensitivity to absolute changes to zero, compared to partial changes -- even larger ones -- that fall short of zero. The results have theoretical implications for theories of progress perception and quantity (in)sensitivity.

Saturation of moral language predicts lower content engagement on social media
Cristian Candia et al.
Nature Human Behaviour, forthcoming

Abstract:
Moral language often travels widely online, but does more moral content always correspond to higher engagement? We analysed 1,621,147 observations across 13 socio-political topics on Twitter (n = 530,104), Reddit (n = 1,048,653) and 8chan (n = 42,390). Using Distributed Dictionary Representations -- word embeddings scored against an expert-validated moral dictionary -- we measured moral loading (that is, a post’s overall moral relevance) and moral density (that is, concentration of moral content across words). Negative-binomial models showed that moral loading was positively associated with engagement (range 1.12 [0.96, 1.28] to 9.07 [8.21, 9.93], all P < 0.001). Conditional on moral loading, however, moral density was ‘negatively’ associated with engagement (range −4.71 [−5.41, −4.02] to −0.40 [−0.52, −0.27], all P < 0.001). Engagement peaked at density 0.30 [0.30048, 0.30070], P < 0.001, with lower engagement below (2.28-fold) and above (2.78-fold), consistent with an engagement advantage for moral language that is bounded by an overmoralization penalty pattern.

The Value-Oriented Dynamics of Support for Universal Basic Income in the United States
Changlip Kim et al.
American Politics Research, forthcoming

Abstract:
Existing research on public support for Universal Basic Income (UBI) has focused on the individual and contextual effects that shape attitudes towards this emerging welfare policy in the United States. New information and persuasive framing seem to do little to change the polarized nature of UBI support. However, previous studies have not considered value-based frames that map UBI to traditional values-based divisions in American politics. We analyze an original, nationally representative survey of American respondents and show that framing UBI in terms of egalitarianism and moral traditionalism strongly influences public opinion towards UBI. Underlying value cleavages drive patterns of acceptance or rejection of UBI framing messages, rather than partisanship. Our findings also suggest that value congruence is a critical part of UBI attitudes: traditional opponents of UBI can be moved to support the policy when they receive a treatment amenable to their values.

The Lay Belief That There is Virtue in Duty and Duty in Virtue: A Novel Lens for Viewing Moral Judgment
Hajin Kim, Julian Zlatev & Dale Miller
Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, forthcoming

Abstract:
We praise the performance of virtuous acts (e.g., composting) and condemn the failure to perform dutiful ones (e.g., littering). Importantly, however, moral acts may contain elements of both virtue and duty. Composting elicits praise, but not composting may also elicit condemnation. Across six studies, we show that a bivalent measure of moral evaluations (assessing the blame or praise for both doing and not doing the same act) allows for more accurate predictions of moral behaviors and provides possible explanations for various existing moral puzzles. Studies 1a to 1c demonstrate that the moral evaluations for, and emotional responses to, doing and not doing an act are not systematically related. Bivalent moral evaluations illuminate why Republicans were less likely to mask than Democrats during the COVID-19 pandemic (Study 2) and why financial compensation can reduce blood donations (Study 3). These evaluations improve predictions of intended blood donations (Study 3) and actual voting behavior (Study 4).

How power shapes judgments of culpability: Shield or liability?
Gerben van Kleef et al.
Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, forthcoming

Abstract:
Powerholders can be the object of great respect and admiration, but they may also be distrusted and “canceled” in the court of public opinion. This raises the question of whether power is an asset or a detriment when one is implicated in wrongdoing. Different theoretical perspectives informed competing hypotheses, suggesting power may either decrease (shielding hypothesis) or increase (liability hypothesis) judgments of culpability. Here, we report four main studies and 10 supplemental studies that addressed this conundrum, using diverse transgressions, methods, and samples. In Study 1, participants judged higher power individuals to be likelier sources of deceitful die-rolling reports than lower power individuals, and they trusted them less in an incentivized behavioral trust game. In Study 2, participants rated higher power people as more probable perpetrators of financial fraud than lower power people, and this effect was mediated by perceived impunity (i.e., powerholders seemingly believing they can get away with anything). Study 3 was an archival study of 97,628 forum posts about diverse transgressions where there was ambiguity about who was the culprit, and users rendered judgments. We found that higher power posters were about twice as likely to be deemed guilty than lower power posters. Finally, Study 4 excluded generic power saliency as an alternative explanation and replicated the mediation via perceived impunity. These findings indicate that, besides many perks, power comes with perils in the form of ascribed culpability.

Diverging Effects of Deliberation: How Perceived Thoughtfulness About Political Issues Affects Character Judgments
Zachary Grey et al.
Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, forthcoming

Abstract:
Across three studies (N = 896), we examined the effects of perceived deliberation and political (dis)agreement on moral character judgments. We tested whether targets who agree or disagree with the participant on a political issue are evaluated more positively when they are described as deliberating (vs. not deliberating). Results showed that in cases of agreement, there was no effect of deliberation on moral character judgments. This was because deliberators were seen as less certain (which was associated with more negative evaluations) but also more thoughtful (which was associated with more positive evaluations). However, in cases of disagreement, deliberation led to more positive moral character judgments. This was because deliberators were again seen as less certain and more thoughtful, but both perceptions were associated with more positive evaluations. These findings suggest that perceived deliberation makes disagreement more palatable and that people are less concerned with how like-minded people reach their conclusions.

A Morality Evolutionary Game Theory Can Model
Mikhail Volkov
Philosophy of Science, October 2026, Pages 898-919

Abstract:
Evolutionary game-theoretic (EGT) models of morality face powerful under-addressed objections. Critics claim the simulations fail to specify their explanandum, muddying their explanatory value. Additionally, morality is suggested to be not computationally representable, jeopardising the method’s general applicability. This paper explicates and addresses the objections. I argue at least one concrete explication of morality, emotionism coupled with functionally understood emotions, can be a plausible subject of EGT explanations. I demonstrate how fixing this explanandum assuages the methodological objections and provide a computational model as proof of concept. If successful, the contribution placates serious long-standing criticisms of evolutionary game theory as a meta-ethical tool.

Moral language often travels widely online, but does more moral content always correspond to higher engagement? We analysed 1,621,147 observations across 13 socio-political topics on Twitter (n = 530,104), Reddit (n = 1,048,653) and 8chan (n = 42,390). Using Distributed Dictionary Representations -- word embeddings scored against an expert-validated moral dictionary -- we measured moral loading (that is, a post’s overall moral relevance) and moral density (that is, concentration of moral content across words). Negative-binomial models showed that moral loading was positively associated with engagement (range 1.12 [0.96, 1.28] to 9.07 [8.21, 9.93], all P < 0.001). Conditional on moral loading, however, moral density was ‘negatively’ associated with engagement (range −4.71 [−5.41, −4.02] to −0.40 [−0.52, −0.27], all P < 0.001). Engagement peaked at density 0.30 [0.30048, 0.30070], P < 0.001, with lower engagement below (2.28-fold) and above (2.78-fold), consistent with an engagement advantage for moral language that is bounded by an overmoralization penalty pattern.

Changlip Kim et al.
American Politics Research, forthcoming

Abstract:
Existing research on public support for Universal Basic Income (UBI) has focused on the individual and contextual effects that shape attitudes towards this emerging welfare policy in the United States. New information and persuasive framing seem to do little to change the polarized nature of UBI support. However, previous studies have not considered value-based frames that map UBI to traditional values-based divisions in American politics. We analyze an original, nationally representative survey of American respondents and show that framing UBI in terms of egalitarianism and moral traditionalism strongly influences public opinion towards UBI. Underlying value cleavages drive patterns of acceptance or rejection of UBI framing messages, rather than partisanship. Our findings also suggest that value congruence is a critical part of UBI attitudes: traditional opponents of UBI can be moved to support the policy when they receive a treatment amenable to their values.

Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, forthcoming

Abstract:

Across six studies, we show that a bivalent measure of moral evaluations (assessing the blame or praise for both doing and not doing the same act) allows for more accurate predictions of moral behaviors and provides possible explanations for various existing moral puzzles. Studies 1a to 1c demonstrate that the moral evaluations for, and emotional responses to, doing and not doing an act are not systematically related. Bivalent moral evaluations illuminate why Republicans were less likely to mask than Democrats during the COVID-19 pandemic (Study 2) and why financial compensation can reduce blood donations (Study 3). How power shapes judgments of culpability: Shield or liability?

Here, we report four main studies and 10 supplemental studies that addressed this conundrum, using diverse transgressions, methods, and samples. A Morality Evolutionary Game Theory Can Model
Mikhail Volkov
Philosophy of Science, October 2026, Pages 898-919

Abstract:
Evolutionary game-theoretic (EGT) models of morality face powerful under-addressed objections. Critics claim the simulations fail to specify their explanandum, muddying their explanatory value. Additionally, morality is suggested to be not computationally representable, jeopardising the method’s general applicability. This paper explicates and addresses the objections. I argue at least one concrete explication of morality, emotionism coupled with functionally understood emotions, can be a plausible subject of EGT explanations. I demonstrate how fixing this explanandum assuages the methodological objections and provide a computational model as proof of concept. item.title: Performing Globalization — Trade and Industry
item.description:
It’s Not (Just) the Tariffs: Rethinking Non-Tariff Measures in a Fragmented Global Economy
Daria Taglioni & Hiau Looi Kee
World Bank Research Observer, August 2026, Pages 223-241

Abstract:
Tariff protection has declined substantially over recent decades, even though tariffs increased in some countries in 2025. Trade restrictions have not disappeared; they have changed form. Non-tariff measures (NTMs) have become central instruments of trade policy, particularly in high-income countries and in highly regulated sectors. Many NTMs pursue legitimate objectives such as food safety, environmental protection, and consumer protection. Yet they also shape market access in less visible ways. Because compliance costs vary widely, NTMs can act as capability-based filters that sort exporters according to regulatory capacity, technological sophistication, and export structure. Drawing on recent advances in estimating ad valorem equivalents (AVEs), this paper examines how the growing importance of NTMs relative to tariffs alters effective protection. Three patterns emerge. Higher-income countries rely relatively more on NTMs than on tariffs; exporters from low- and middle-income countries face higher effective protection in advanced markets; and NTMs disproportionately burden smaller firms, increasing the likelihood of export exit and potentially contributing to greater market concentration. Together, these mutually reinforcing patterns highlight the importance of transparency, careful policy design, and regulatory cooperation to ensure NTMs achieve legitimate objectives without reinforcing fragmentation or inequality in global trade.

Closing Ranks: Organized Labor and Immigration
Carlo Medici
Journal of Political Economy, forthcoming

Abstract:
This paper shows that immigration fostered the emergence of American organized labor. I digitize archival records to assemble the ﬁrst county-level dataset on historical U.S. unionization and use a shift-share instrument to isolate plausibly exogenous labor supply shocks induced by immigration, between 1900 and 1920. Counties with higher immigration experienced increases in union presence and membership. These effects were more pronounced among skilled workers, particularly in counties more exposed to immigrant labor competition, and in areas with more negative attitudes toward immigrants. The evidence is consistent with existing workers unionizing in response to immigration, driven by economic and social motivations.

Gender-Role Traditionalism and Opposition to Trade in the United States
Andrew Kerner & Jane Sumner
PS: Political Science & Politics, forthcoming

Abstract:
A recently popular line in American trade politics is that free trade threatens male blue-collar manufacturing employment, thereby undermining “traditional” family gender roles in which men work outside of the home and women work as caregivers within it. This study asks whether American mass politics mirrors these ideas. Does a preference for “traditional” gender roles lead Americans to protectionism? Our analysis of American National Election Studies data suggests that it does. We find a significant and highly robust empirical relationship between gender conservatism and protectionism. That relationship has been evident since 2008 and it decidedly is not a product of Trump-era politics. That relationship holds among men and women and among Republicans and Democrats, and it is robust to the inclusion of controls meant to isolate gender conservatism from other expressions of conservatism. The recent rise of gender-conservative trade skepticism should be understood as elite politics catching up with the public rather than leading it.

Why is trade not free? A revealed preference approach
Rodrigo Adão et al.
Econometrica, forthcoming

Abstract:
A prominent explanation for why trade is not free is politicians’ desire to protect some of their constituents at the expense of others. In this paper we develop a methodology that can be used to reveal the welfare weights that a nation’s import tariffs implicitly place on different groups of society. Applied in the context of the United States in 2017, this method implies that redistributive trade protection accounts for about a third of US tariff variation and that it causes large monetary transfers between US individuals, mostly driven by differences in welfare weights across sectors of employment. In terms of political economy mechanisms, the welfare weights that we estimate are consistent with lobbying being a significant driver of US trade protection. Perhaps surprisingly, swing states in US presidential elections play a much smaller role.

The Role of Trade in Premature Deindustrialization and Industry Polarization
Michael Sposi, Kei-Mu Yi & Jing Zhang
Econometrica, September 2026, Pages 1779-1815

Abstract:
We document two key patterns of structural change: premature deindustrialization and rising industry polarization. Using a dynamic open-economy model with sector-biased technological change (SBTC), we evaluate the role of trade in these shifts. Trade alone does not cause premature deindustrialization, but its interaction with SBTC -- transmitting global technological change, amplifying the decline in manufacturing's relative price over time, and generating manufacturing trade imbalances across countries -- deepens premature deindustrialization over time. Industry polarization, by contrast, emerges only through trade-driven specialization, as countries diverge along lines of comparative advantage.

Shipping to America
Xiwen Bai et al.
NBER Working Paper, September 2026

Abstract:
We study the macroeconomic and trade-policy implications of disruptions to U.S.-bound shipping routes. Standard models treat them as iceberg-cost shocks, conflating the shock with the response to it. Using satellite vessel-tracking data, we construct route-level measures of potential and effective capacity for all U.S.-bound container ships from 2016 to 2025. Utilization losses in recent disruptions ran 20 to 40 percentage points, and began months before port congestion became visible. We embed these measures in a general equilibrium model in which firms reallocate a common fleet without internalizing the congestion they create and price above marginal cost, while importers' sourcing responds to route profitability. The reallocation triggered by a disruption then has first-order welfare effects, and the route's Domar weight is not a sufficient statistic for its welfare cost. The 2021 West Coast crisis and the 2023-2024 Red Sea attacks cost 0.69% and 0.35% of output. Naval protection of Red Sea shipping generated benefits of 0.04-0.08% of output at a fiscal cost of 0.02%. Tariffs decongest the routes they tax, offsetting or even reversing their conventional welfare cost.

Borrowing in the Shadow of China
Illenin Kondo, César Sosa-Padilla & Zachary Swaziek
NBER Working Paper, September 2026

Abstract:
China's rise as a major lender to emerging economies since the early 2000s has introduced a unique form of lender power: borrowers cannot default on the subsidized loans they receive, but may still face sudden rollover demands outside their control. We argue this distinctive structure -- bilateral rollover risk without default risk -- disciplines recipient countries' borrowing on international markets. In a quantitative long-term sovereign debt model, we show that such rollover-prone nondefaultable Chinese loans expose market debt to dilution risk: governments may need to tap international lenders when repayment to China comes due, and therefore choose to deleverage from private markets when Chinese inflows arrive. Market debt and bond yield dynamics in the data are consistent with this “disciplining effect.” We then use the model to study two geopolitical scenarios: a bloc-formation exercise in which China offers take-it-or-leave-it loans to induce the borrower's exit from international debt markets, and an optimal exposure-to-China problem under the risk of a permanent and sudden retrenchment of Chinese funding. Together, these results show how official finance à la China can simultaneously improve market borrowing conditions and become a new destabilizing force to the global sovereign debt architecture as geopolitical alliances shift.

item.title: How Typical — Stereotypes and Norms
item.description:
Why Most Stereotypes Are Negative
Christian Unkelbach, Anne Irena Weitzel & Hans Alves
Psychological Review, forthcoming

Abstract:
Stereotypes are a foundational construct in psychological science, often defined as beliefs concerning characteristic group attributes. We present a cognitive-ecological theory of social perception that predicts and explains why such characteristic attributes are likely negative, that is, why most stereotypes are negative. The theory assumes that, cognitively, people characterize groups by attributes that distinguish them from other groups. Ecologically, positive social information is more frequent (i.e., positivity prevalence), and negative social information is more diverse (i.e., negativity diversity). If negative attributes are less frequent and more diverse relative to positive attributes, then they must be more likely to distinguish one group from another. Consequently, the attributes people see as characteristic of a group are likely to be negative. We illustrate the predicted stereotype negativity across two studies and two existing data sets. We then formalize the theory and illustrate it with simulations showing that rare attributes can be highly diagnostic of group membership while applying to only a minority of group members. Thus, the theory explains why most stereotype content is likely negative, despite the well-documented positivity prevalence, and why stereotypes may be diagnostic and comparatively accurate, despite being descriptively inaccurate. The theory explains stereotype negativity without requiring motivational derogation, essentialist group differences, or a general negativity bias, and it clarifies when positive stereotypes should occur. We also discuss the theory’s relation to dimensional models of stereotype content and consequences for interventions aimed at reducing stereotype negativity.

“A girl is the champion!”: Well-intentioned gendered messages can backfire
April Bailey, Maya Kreitman & Andrei Cimpian
Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, October 2026, Pages 2581-2600

Abstract:
Initiatives aimed at promoting gender equity in majority-male domains often emphasize gender to highlight women’s achievements (e.g., “Space4Women,” “all-women spacewalk”). Does such gendered messaging help achieve equity goals? Two theoretical accounts offer competing predictions. An informational account suggests that referencing a gender alongside a domain should strengthen beliefs that the referenced gender participates and succeeds. A pragmatic account, however, predicts that explicitly marking gender may backfire by signaling that the referenced gender is atypical in the domain -- otherwise, why mention it? We tested these two possibilities with U.S. children (ages 4–10; N = 326) and adults (N = 788). Participants learned about fictional activities described with either gendered messaging (e.g., “A girl/boy is the Gazzer champion”) or control messaging (e.g., “Joan/Rob is the Gazzer champion”). Gendered messaging backfired compared to control messaging on average, causing participants to infer lower participation by the referenced gender and, among adults, lower ability. Gendered messaging also undermined participants’ interest in the activities. A meta-analysis across experiments revealed small-to-moderate effects that were larger for adults than children, consistent with developmental changes in pragmatic reasoning. Finally, backfire effects disappeared for messaging about fictional groups, suggesting that background knowledge about the referenced group may be needed to trigger pragmatic inferences. Together, these findings advance theoretical accounts of pragmatic reasoning while indicating that well-intentioned gendered messaging may paradoxically undermine equity goals. A more effective alternative may be to clearly feature women in a domain without explicitly framing it as being “for them.”

On Confederate Monuments, Their Removal and Racial Bias
Maximilian Primbs et al.
Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, forthcoming

Abstract:
The presence of Confederate monuments and their removal has been a frequent topic of societal discussion in the United States. Taking a situational perspective (i.e. the Bias of Crowds model), the present paper investigated whether the presence of Confederate monuments and their removal from an area causally affect the racial biases of people in that area. Across multiple large-scale data analyses (N1 = 1,753,557), online experiments (N2a = 1,164, N2b = 416, N3 = 537), and a field study (N4 = 176), we found no evidence that the presence or removal of Confederate monuments reliably affects the implicit (or explicit) racial biases of people. We discuss implications for situational models of bias and best research practices for conducting geographical difference studies.

Wrestling with perceptions: How WWE live events in Saudi Arabia shaped views of Muslims in the United States
Rudy Alamillo
Politics, Groups, and Identities, forthcoming

Abstract:
In 2018, the Saudi Ministry of Sport and WWE announced a 10-year agreement to host multiple WWE events in Saudi Arabia to be broadcast around the world. Although these events were intended to drive tourism to Saudi Arabia, they may also have improved attitudes toward Muslims among WWE fans in line with the parasocial contact hypothesis, which argues that positive exposure to members of a minority group through the media can improve feelings toward that group. I test this proposition using two studies. First, an analysis of tweets from professional wrestling fans suggests that relative to fans of another professional wrestling company, WWE fans saw a substantial increase in positive posts about Muslims following WWE's events in Saudi Arabia. Second, using an online survey experiment, I find that exposure to WWE events in Saudi Arabia increased feelings of commonality toward Muslims among WWE fans, which is a key mechanism through which attitude change occurs. Taken together, these results improve our understanding of the parasocial contact hypothesis and provide evidence that under certain conditions, attitude change can occur not just via exposure to positive depictions of well-known members of outgroups, but incidental exposure to outgroups members as well.

The Politics of Black Classification: Sociopolitical Cues and Racial Perception
Lauren Davenport, Hakeem Jefferson & Hunter Rendleman
Perspectives on Politics, forthcoming

Abstract:
What makes someone Black in American society today? From Donald Trump questioning Kamala Harris’s racial identity to Joe Biden’s claim that hesitant Black voters “ain’t Black,” American politics frequently brings questions of racial authenticity and belonging to the surface. Yet political science often approaches race as a fixed attribute, rather than a social construction. Here, we seek to understand how Americans define blackness in social and political life. Using a conjoint experiment with a racially diverse sample that includes Black, White, and mixed-race Black-White respondents, we evaluate how ascribed and acquired traits influence perceptions of blackness. The results show that inherited characteristics -- particularly parentage and skin tone, which are the strongest determinants of racial classification -- play a central role, yet sociopolitical cues such as partisanship, neighborhood context, and spousal race also influence racial classification. Using a continuous measure, we also show that respondents make graded assessments of blackness rather than purely binary classifications, with some individuals perceived as more Black than others. Black respondents are more likely than White respondents to classify a broader set of profiles as Black, consistent with a more inclusive understanding of racial membership; however, they also place greater emphasis on shared political identity. These findings clarify how racial categories are socially constructed and why that construction carries real political and social consequences.

Perceived Pandemic Deficits: How COVID-19 Stereotypes Influence Interview Judgments
Cody Cox et al.
Journal of Applied Social Psychology, forthcoming

Abstract:
Following the COVID-19 pandemic, the perception that high school and college students' social skills had been negatively affected by the social-distancing lockdown proliferated. These perceptions may impact the ability of these individuals to succeed in interview settings. In the current study, participants with hiring experience (N = 322) rated a recorded interview and were told the applicant's social skills either had been impacted by the COVID-19 lockdown or that the lockdown had not impacted social skills (in reality, the interview was recorded before the pandemic). Results indicated that participants rated the applicant's interview performance (i.e., eye contact), personality, and potential hireability more poorly when told that COVID-19 impacted social skills as compared to the stereotype mitigation condition. These results were even stronger for extraverted participants, consistent with research indicating that extraverts draw stronger inferences from applicants' eye contact. Our study demonstrates that stereotypes about lockdown during the COVID-19 pandemic harming social development impacted perceived interview performance and that these stereotypes can be mitigated with additional information.

Credible Prejudice? When and Why Mainstream Party Adoption of Far-Right Rhetoric Weakens Anti-Prejudice Norms
Ali Karčić
Political Behavior, forthcoming

Abstract:
This article examines whether mainstream political parties adopt prejudiced rhetoric from the far right and how such shifts shape anti-prejudice norms. Building on existing work, I argue that mainstream parties are particularly influential in weakening anti-prejudice norms because they possess greater normative credibility and legitimacy than far-right parties. Empirically, the article combines cross-national observational evidence with two preregistered survey experiments in Germany and Denmark. Using parliamentary speeches from six European countries between 1994 and 2022, I document rising mainstream party anti-Muslim rhetoric and its association with weaker norms against holding far-right views. The experiments provide causal evidence for the argument. In Germany, exposure to prejudiced rhetoric weakens anti-prejudice norms, but only when voiced by mainstream parties, rather than far right parties, likely due to their normative credibility and legitimacy. In Denmark, comparable effects are absent, consistent with decades of mainstream accommodation having already normalized such rhetoric. The experimental results also show that rhetoric targeting Muslims weakens anti-prejudice norms toward out-groups more broadly, suggesting spillover effects. These findings have important implications for future scholarship: when mainstream parties adopt prejudiced rhetoric from the far right, they affect not only electoral politics, but also the broader social norm environment.
